prize_parts.citation: For the development of base editing, the programmable chemical conversion of DNA bases without double-strand cleavage
For the development of targeted protein degradation by heterobifunctional PROTAC molecules

statement.case_for: I keep base editing first and now pair it with targeted protein degradation, because together they are the two achievements on the shortlist where a chemically defined, designed molecule gave researchers and clinicians a capability they did not have. Base editors turn a deaminase reaction into a programmable edit on one base pair without a double-strand break, and are already in patients. PROTACs turn induced proximity into a general modality for removing proteins that have no active site to inhibit, and the 2001 Crews-Deshaies concept has been taken up across medicinal chemistry and chemical biology. Both are explainable in one sentence, are mechanistically well understood, and have been reproduced widely. Pairing them also fits the three-person limit cleanly (Liu; Crews and Deshaies) and places the prize in chemical biology, which the committee has not recognised since the 2020 and 2022 prizes touched this area from other directions.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this configuration is an attribution compromise. Dropping Komor and Gaudelli, who wrote the two decisive base-editor papers, and Handa, whose cereblon discovery underlies the molecular-glue branch, leaves out people with defensible claims to make the numbers fit. There is also a timing risk on both parts: genome editing already has the 2020 prize, and no PROTAC is yet an approved drug, so the clinical proof is incomplete. If the committee insists on a complete picture of credit, delivery chemistry (B013) or sequencing (B058) are mature, clinically validated alternatives with fewer open questions about maturity.

responses.point: Aqvist ranks PROTACs first as a game-changing chemical modality and puts base editing second with Liu alone, treating Komor and Gaudelli as lead trainees.
responses.response: I agree with the single-laureate framing for base editing and have moved toward it from my opening trio, because it frees a seat for the degrader part without breaching the three-person limit. I disagree mildly that Komor and Gaudelli are simply trainees: Gaudelli's evolution of a DNA-acting adenine deaminase was a real chemical advance, so the cost of this choice should be stated openly in the citation rather than ignored. I share his view that the PROTAC branch is slightly early clinically, which is why I would anchor the citation on the 2001 concept and not on approvals.

responses.point: Linke ranks base editing first with Liu, Komor and Gaudelli following the primary record, would press the Nishida-Kondo priority question, and would split the PROTAC credit between the original concept and the cereblon and VHL work.
responses.response: I agree that the Liu-Komor-Gaudelli trio follows the primary record most faithfully and I would support it if the committee prefers a single-achievement prize. I do not think Nishida and Kondo's Target-AID work, which fused a deaminase to a Cas nickase in a different architecture, is enough to displace the Liu lab as the work that generalised the approach. On PROTACs, I take his point that Handa and Ciulli matter, but splitting the credit across four or five names makes the part unwinnable under the three-person cap, so I would credit the original concept and let the citation wording acknowledge the molecular-glue branch.

responses.point: Chabes ranks base editing first, argues Liu-lab work generalised the approach and excludes Nishida and Kondo, and values PROTAC degradation as measurable, rationally designed chemistry.
responses.response: We agree on base editing and on the chemical logic of both achievements. I would qualify his comfort with the PROTAC trio: his own note says the Handa addition is a compromise, and I accept that, but I think the cleaner choice is to honour the conceptual origin (Crews and Deshaies) than to hold a seat for cereblon. Where I go beyond him is in not giving sequencing (B058) a prize seat; its impact is undeniable but I read it as mature technology that is overdue rather than as the strongest chemical-design story this year.

responses.point: Sparr ranks ionizable lipid nanoparticles first for the Cullis, Hope and Madden formulation work, noting the pKa-tuned physical chemistry behind delivery and the overlap with the 2023 Medicine prize.
responses.response: I find her physical-chemical case for B013 compelling and I ranked it third myself; delivery is the reason mRNA and siRNA drugs work. My reservation is attribution: six names across several groups and a Vancouver-centred trio that leaves out Anderson, Langer and MacLachlan, plus a medicine-versus-chemistry framing risk after 2023. I would hold B013 as my first alternative and would support it if base editing and degraders both stall, but I do not yet see a trio that survives scrutiny of the credit.

responses.point: Brzezinski ranks nitrogenase first as a mature structure-plus-mechanism achievement and places base editing fourth, questioning the third laureate seat and noting CRISPR was honoured in 2020.
responses.response: I respect the nitrogenase case as classical chemistry with stable structures, but I rank it outside my top eight because the decisive credit is spread over structural and kinetic groups and the catalytic cycle remains debated, which makes a short citation hard. I accept his concern about CRISPR overlap and the third seat, and that is exactly why I now propose Liu alone for B024: it keeps the citation focused on the chemical conversion of bases and avoids the third-seat dispute.

uncertainties: Whether the committee views base editing as a distinct chemical advance or as a follow-on to the 2020 CRISPR prize.
Whether crediting Crews and Deshaies without Handa, Ciulli or Gray is defensible, and whether the 2001 priority claim is as strong as recalled; I cannot verify details here.
Whether the lack of an approved PROTAC drug makes degraders premature this year.
Whether two achievements from chemical biology and drug modality are better than a single base-editing prize naming Liu, Komor and Gaudelli.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile: my postdoc mentors (Molly Stevens, Freddy Boey) and Linkoping colleagues are not credited names on the shortlist. I note only overlapping research interests with Emma Sparr in self-assembly and peptide systems, which are not tied to any shortlisted candidate.
